classification.difficultyReason: Choose integer roots and repeatedly apply the factor theorem and long division, then use the quadratic formula or exclude non-real roots; these are routine linked procedures explicitly taught in the preceding examples.

answer.short:
$x=3,\ 2-\sqrt5,\ 2+\sqrt5$.

Use the factor theorem, then the quadratic formula.
answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^3-7x^2+11x+3$.
$$P(3)=27-63+33+3=0.$$
Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x-3)(x^2-4x-1).$$
Thus $x=3$ or $x^2-4x-1=0$. For the quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{(-4)^2-4(1)(-1)}}{2}\\x&=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{20}}2\\x&=2\pm\sqrt5.\end{align*}$$
The solutions are $x=3,\ 2-\sqrt5,\ 2+\sqrt5$.

answer.short:
$x=-1$.

The remaining quadratic has negative discriminant.
answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^3+4x^2+10x+7$.
$$P(-1)=-1+4-10+7=0.$$
Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x+1)(x^2+3x+7).$$
For the quadratic, $\Delta=3^2-4(1)(7)=-19<0$, so it has no real roots.
Thus the only real solution is $x=-1$.

answer.short:
$x=0,\ 2,\ 3,\ \frac{-3-\sqrt{13}}2,\ \frac{-3+\sqrt{13}}2$.

Remove the common factor, use the factor theorem, then solve the remaining quadratic.
answer.worked:
Take out $x$ and let $Q(x)=x^4-2x^3-10x^2+23x-6$.
$$Q(2)=16-16-40+46-6=0.$$
Long division gives $Q(x)=(x-2)R(x)$, where $R(x)=x^3-10x+3$.
$$R(3)=27-30+3=0.$$
Dividing $R(x)$ by $x-3$ gives
$$R(x)=(x-3)(x^2+3x-1).$$
The original equation becomes
$$x(x-2)(x-3)(x^2+3x-1)=0.$$
For the quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{3^2-4(1)(-1)}}2\\x&=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{13}}2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=0,\ 2,\ 3,\ \frac{-3-\sqrt{13}}2,\ \frac{-3+\sqrt{13}}2$.

answer.short:
$x=-1,\ 1,\ 2$.

Use the factor theorem; the final quadratic has no real roots.
